title: Running Best
focus: Keep one number as you sweep. Keep one stack as you sweep. Keep one capacity as you fill.

cards.title: Kadane's Algorithm
cards.trigger: Maximum or minimum contiguous subarray, with negatives in play.
cards.recall: Write Kadane from memory. Then answer: what does `cur` mean at each step, why is it `max(x, cur + x)` and not `max(cur, cur + x)`, and how does the all-negative case still work?
useWhen: Maximum subarray sum
Maximum product subarray, carry both max and min
Best single buy and sell, which is Kadane on the difference array
Circular maximum subarray, total minus the minimum subarray
Any 'best contiguous run' phrasing
template: cur = max(x, cur + x)      # restart at x, or extend the run
best = max(best, cur)      # global answer is tracked separately
# Product variant: a negative flips min into max, so carry both
if x < 0: hi, lo = lo, hi
# Circular: answer is max(kadane_max, total - kadane_min)
# unless every element is negative, in which case it is kadane_max
keyInsights: `cur` is the best subarray *ending exactly here*. That definition is why the restart branch is `x` alone
Initialising to 0 instead of `nums[0]` breaks the all-negative case, which is the standard hidden test
The circular version has one special case, all negatives, where total minus min is the empty subarray
cards.trap: 'Return the indices, not the sum.' Track the start whenever you restart, and commit it whenever you update the global best. Retrofit this and you will get it wrong.

cards.title: Monotonic Stack
cards.trigger: For each element, find the nearest element to one side that is bigger or smaller.
cards.recall: Write next-greater from memory. Then answer: when you pop an index, whose answer are you filling in, and why is total work linear despite the inner while loop?
useWhen: Next or previous greater or smaller element
Daily temperatures, stock span
Largest rectangle in a histogram, and maximal rectangle in a matrix
Trapping rain water
Remove k digits to make the smallest number
template: # Next greater to the right. Stack holds indices with decreasing values.
out[stack.pop()] = x      # x is the answer for that popped index
# Histogram: sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack
keyInsights: You are not computing the answer for the current element, you are resolving answers for elements you parked earlier
Each index is pushed once and popped once, so the while loop is amortised O(1). Say it that way
The sentinel at the end is not a hack, it is what guarantees every parked index gets resolved
cards.trap: 'Make it circular.' Iterate the array twice with `i % n` and do not push on the second pass. If you push twice you corrupt the stack.

cards.title: Global vs Returned Value
cards.trigger: The best answer might pass *through* a node without going up to its parent.
cards.recall: Write the diameter function from memory. Then answer the pattern's whole point: why must the value you return differ from the value you record, and what would break if they were the same?
useWhen: Tree diameter, longest path between any two nodes
Maximum path sum where the path can bend at a node
Longest univalue or increasing path
Largest BST subtree
Any tree problem where the answer is not rooted at the root
template: # Diameter: the answer bends at some node, but the parent can only use one arm
best = max(best, l + r)          # RECORD: the bend, both arms
return 1 + max(l, r)             # RETURN: one arm, for the parent
# Max path sum: same shape, plus clamp negative arms to zero
l = max(gain(node.left), 0)          # a negative arm is worse than no arm
keyInsights: A path through a node uses both children. A path continuing to the parent can use only one. That asymmetry is the entire pattern
Recognise it by the phrase 'between any two nodes' rather than 'from the root'
Clamping to zero is how you say 'I would rather take nothing than take a negative subtree'
cards.trap: 'Return the path itself.' You now need parent links or to thread the path through the recursion, and the elegant version does not extend for free.

cards.title: 0/1 Knapsack
patterns: Each item used at most once
cards.trigger: A fixed set of items, a capacity, and each item is either in or out.
cards.recall: Write the 1D rolled version from memory. Then answer the question that separates 0/1 from unbounded: why does the capacity loop run *backwards*, and what happens if it runs forwards?
useWhen: Subset sum, partition into equal halves
Target sum with plus and minus signs, after a transform
Maximum value under a weight budget
Count subsets hitting an exact total
Last stone weight II, minimise the difference
template: # dp[c] = True if some subset of items seen so far sums to exactly c
for c in range(target, x - 1, -1):   # BACKWARDS
# Value version: dp[c] = best value achievable with capacity c
# Counting version: dp[c] += dp[c - x], same backwards loop
keyInsights: Backwards keeps `dp[c - x]` at its previous-item value, so item x is used at most once. Forwards is the unbounded knapsack
That single loop direction is the only structural difference between the two knapsack families. Memorise it as a pair
This is pseudo-polynomial. If the capacity is huge the table is huge, and saying that shows you understand the bound
cards.trap: 'Now each item has unlimited copies.' Flip the loop to forwards. If you cannot explain why in one sentence, you memorised code instead of the idea.

cards.title: Bellman-Ford
cards.trigger: Negative edge weights, or a hard limit on the number of hops.
cards.recall: Write the k-stops version from memory. Then answer: why do you relax from a *snapshot* of the previous round rather than in place, and what does relaxing in place actually compute?
useWhen: Shortest path with negative edges
At most k edges or k stops
Detect a negative cycle, currency arbitrage
Small graphs where E log V beats nothing and simplicity wins
Any constraint on path *length in edges*
template: # Cheapest flight with at most k stops = at most k+1 edges
def cheapest(n, flights, src, dst, k):
snap = dist[:]                 # freeze the previous round
for u, v, w in flights:
if snap[u] + w < dist[v]:  # read snap, write dist
return -1 if dist[dst] == INF else dist[dst]
# Full Bellman-Ford: V-1 rounds, then one extra round to detect negatives
for u, v, w in edges:
for u, v, w in edges:
keyInsights: The snapshot enforces 'at most one more edge per round'. In place, one round can chain many edges and blow past k
After round i, dist holds the best path using at most i edges. That is the invariant and it is worth saying
One extra relaxing round that still improves something proves a reachable negative cycle
cards.trap: 'Why not Dijkstra with a stop count in the state?' You can, but the state is (node, stops) and you must not settle on node alone. Explaining that shows real understanding.
